title: The sower (Matthew 13:1–9)
hook: seed lands on path, rock, thorns and good soil; most is wasted, and the harvest is huge anyway
tomorrow: The mustard seed and the yeast (Matthew 13:31–33)

segments.voice: Yesterday, parable: a small story thrown alongside something too big to look at straight. Today, the first of them.

A farmer walks the edge of his field, a bag of seed on his hip. He takes a handful and flings it in a wide arc. He isn't placing seeds. He's throwing. Some lands on the hard footpath, and the birds have it before he finishes the row. Some lands where rock sits under a skin of soil: it shoots up fast, and the first hot day kills it. Some lands among thorns and gets strangled. And some lands in good ground. Plenty of the listeners had done this with their own hands. They knew how much seed a farmer loses. They didn't expect the ending.
screen: `A FARMER THROWING SEED.` → `PATH, ROCK, THORNS, GOOD GROUND.` → `THEY DIDN'T EXPECT THE ENDING.`

segments.voice: It opens, in the King James: "Behold, a sower went forth to sow." Three kinds of ground out of four fail. Keep count and it's a story about waste. Then the last line: the good ground "brought forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold." Some readers hear a hundredfold as the kind of number that makes a farmer laugh out loud. Everyone knew about failure. The surprise is a harvest that dwarfs it. Later in the same chapter, the Gospel gives an explanation, told to the disciples. The seed is the word, the good news of God's kingdom. The grounds are kinds of listeners: one hears and loses it at once, one is thrilled for a week, one lets worries choke it, one lets it grow. Christians hear the story from two sides, sometimes both at once. About the sower: keep throwing, even when most of it seems wasted, because you can't see where the good ground is. About the soil: what kind of ground am I, today? And notice: the farmer doesn't test the soil or save his seed for the good patch. He throws it on path, rock and thorns, as if there's plenty to go around. It ends: "Who hath ears to hear, let him hear." The story stops, and hands the question to you.
screen: `A SOWER WENT FORTH TO SOW` · `THREE GROUNDS OUT OF FOUR FAIL` · `A HUNDREDFOLD` · `THE SOWER, OR THE SOIL?` · then, large: `HE THROWS IT EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Let your breathing slow, and picture the four grounds: the hard path, too trampled to take anything in; thin soil over rock; the thorns, plenty of life but the worries winning; the good earth, open and ready. Without grading yourself, notice which one you are today. It's only today: ground changes, paths get broken up, thorns get pulled, so let yourself be whatever ground you are.
The sower. A farmer throwing seed everywhere, as if there's plenty, and a harvest that dwarfs the waste.
Your line: keep throwing seed. That's the first story of Camp 2, and day twenty-three, done.

screen: `DAY 23 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MUSTARD SEED AND THE YEAST.`

howItsDone: The parable of the sower is told in Matthew, Mark and Luke and read aloud in churches; Christians hear it as a question about how they receive the word, and as encouragement to keep sharing it.

original.note: Greek: "the one sowing," from speirō, to scatter seed.

what a scholar hears: Matthew 13:18–23 adds an explanation, told to the disciples: the seed is the word of the kingdom, the grounds are kinds of hearers. and some readers hear the hundredfold as meant to astonish.

chat.says: Isn't the sower story kind of sad? Most of the seed dies.
options: Most is lost, but the good ground's harvest is far bigger than the waste.
Not really, because in the story most of the seed grows just fine.
It is sad, and the lesson is to only plant where you're sure.
chat.meaning: Three kinds of ground out of four fail, but the good ground gives thirty, sixty, a hundredfold: a harvest that dwarfs the waste.

sower.meaning: someone who scatters seed by hand to plant a field

hundredfold.meaning: a hundred times as much as was sown
